Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff put a proposal to Washington on 3 November 1943 about who should run the war in the Mediterranean. At the time, General Eisenhower ran the central part, while a separate commander in Cairo ran the east and the Balkans.

The paper argues that split command caused delays, since moving even small forces needed approval from the Combined Chiefs of Staff, and chances in the Aegean had been lost that way. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d287:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a long secret telegram from Washington on 22 November 1943. Its lead item is Turkey's official reply, reported by Ambassador Steinhardt, to Anthony Eden's recent proposals that Turkey grant air bases and move toward war.

Ankara refuses the bases, holding that granting them means war with Germany whatever Britain thinks, and that the minimum arms promised at Adana were never supplied. Coastal cities and industries would be destroyed, Turkey warns, leaving her a liability, not an asset. Hull adds von Papen's threat of a German and Bulgarian attack within days. He adds Finland's tighter turn toward Germany and Portuguese coolness over the Azores. He ends with a French committee vote to recall Helleu from Lebanon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d387:
President Roosevelt handed Marshal Stalin a secret written proposal at Tehran on 29 November 1943. It restated what the American delegation had proposed at the Moscow Conference about air bases in the Soviet Union. It is one of three such papers Roosevelt gave Stalin that day.

The proposal asks that American aircraft on shuttle-bombing runs from the United Kingdom be allowed to refuel, make emergency repairs, and rearm at Soviet bases. It also seeks a better mutual exchange of weather information and improved signal and air communication between the two countries. Roosevelt records his understanding on two points. Moscow agreed to these ideas in principle at the Moscow Conference. And Soviet authorities would be told to meet his military mission to work out the concrete measures. He hopes the arrangements can be made promptly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d487:

Churchill often used Hopkins as his fastest route to Roosevelt. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Hopkins lived in the White House and carried messages no formal channel could match for speed or candor. A Churchill note to him is summit diplomacy at its most personal: one leader reaching the other through a trusted friend. Readers get a glimpse of how much of the alliance ran on this single relationship, bypassing embassies and foreign offices entirely.
frus-1944-quebec-d87: Document 87 is where the editors, not the wartime officials, speak. The entry is an editorial note in the Quebec 1944 volume. frus-1944-quebec-d187:
Cherwell also recorded the lend-lease conversation of September 14, 1944, between Roosevelt and Churchill. With Germany beaten, Britain hoped food, shipping, and munitions would keep coming during the war against Japan to cover reasonable needs. Roosevelt indicated assent, but Morgenthau pressed for definite figures rather than proportional aid.

The figures discussed were about 3.5 billion dollars of munitions aid in the first year and 3 billion in other supplies, offset by reverse lend-lease. All supplies would be on lend-lease terms. There would be no conditions jeopardizing Britain's export recovery, and no lend-lease articles could be exported. Roosevelt himself added the words "or sold for profit." A joint committee, informal at first and headed by Morgenthau, would work out the details.
frus-1944-quebec-d287:
The final report of the Combined Chiefs, C.C.S. 680/2, was submitted to Roosevelt and Churchill on September 16, 1944. It is the approved version of the draft the leaders had amended in plenary the day before. The over-all objective now reads as the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan, sharpened from the draft's broader phrase about the Axis Powers.

The strategic concept and undertakings follow the draft, with small telling changes. French and Italian forces are to be assisted against Germany and/or Japan. Other co-belligerents are helped against "the enemy Powers." The redeployment sentence carries the compromise wording settled during the week: highest priority, having regard to other agreed and/or inescapable commitments. The report closed the conference's military business.
