Burnet was a rigorous Scottish classicist who believed the fragments deserved exact, unsentimental reading.

His study set the standard for English scholarship on the Presocratics for generations, and his reconstructions still anchor debate. Readable despite its learning, the book follows arguments about change, being, and the kosmos as they pass from teacher to critic. Readers looking for where Western reason begins will find its birthplace mapped here.
tob-9287:
Buehler's translation of the Laws of Manu is the classic English form of ancient India's great law-book. Manu, the primeval lawgiver of legend, orders society by dharma: the duties of castes, the stages of life from student to hermit, and the king's justice. Georg Buehler rendered it for the Sacred Books of the East.

Marriage, inheritance, diet, penance, and the treatment of women and servants all receive rules. The code shaped Hindu law and custom for centuries, and modern India still argues with its legacy. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Buehler's version remains the scholars' standard.
kabbalah-unveiled-mathers-1887:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers, a founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, published The Kabbalah Unveiled in 1887. The book translates three key parts of the Zohar, the central work of Jewish mysticism, from Latin into English. It was the first English version of any part of the Zohar.

The three books are the Book of Concealed Mystery and the Greater and Lesser Holy Assemblies. They picture the divine nature through the ten sephiroth and vast symbolic faces of God. Mathers adds a long introduction mapping the Kabbalistic system for beginners. The translation fed the whole modern occult revival in the English-speaking world.
weishaupt-kurze-rechtfertigung-1787:
Adam Weishaupt founded the Illuminati in Bavaria in 1776 and was driven from his post when the state turned on the order. After officials seized the group's papers and printed them to shame him, he answered in print himself. Kurze Rechtfertigung meiner Absichten, issued in 1787, is that answer, a short book in his own voice.

Weishaupt replies point by point to the charges drawn from the seized letters. He says the papers were picked and arranged to make him look like a fraud and a corrupter of youth. He then sets out what he claims he truly meant the order to do. Few books from the affair speak so plainly for the losing side.
system-und-folgen-illuminatenordens-1787:
System und Folgen des Illuminatenordens was printed at Munich in 1787, as the Bavarian state moved against the Illuminati. The book draws its case from the order's own printed papers, seized in house searches such as the raid on Zwack's home. It presents the state's reading in the form of letters.

Letter by letter, the writer lays out the order's grades, rules, and secret aims. He then warns what such a hidden system could do to church, state, and public trust. The book served as a guide to the seized archive for readers of the day. It shows how officials turned private letters into a public charge.
schottmuller-untergang-templer-vol1-1887:
Konrad Schottmüller, a German historian, told the fall of the Templar order from its own records in 1887. Der Untergang des Templer-Ordens, volume one, is the narrative half of his great study. It follows the order from the mass arrests of 1307 to its end.

Schottmüller walks through the charges, the papal inquiry, and the slow crush of the defense. He builds each claim on the trial papers his second volume prints. The story ends with the order suppressed in 1312 and its master burned in 1314. The book remains the great nineteenth-century history of the affair.
schottmuller-untergang-templer-vol2-1887:
Urkunden is the title of Schottmüller's second volume, and it means what it says: the documents themselves. Printed in 1887 as the mate to his narrative history, it publishes the Templar trial records in full. The narrative tells the story; this volume shows the proof.

Charters, interrogations, and official acts fill the pages in their record form. Scholars cite these texts when they test any claim about the order's fall. The pair of volumes split the work cleanly, story in one and sources in the other. Few studies of the Templars can be used without this file of papers.
gibson-monsters-of-the-sea-1887:
John Gibson ranged the whole sea monster shelf in Monsters of the Sea, printed in 1887. His survey runs from the kraken and the sea serpent to the giant squid. Gibson writes for the broad Victorian reader who loved a wonder with a fact in it.

He marks each tale as legend or as truth, and tells why he judges it so. The book hops from Norse myth to fresh reports from steamship decks. Its charm is its range: the deep as one great cabinet of beasts. The volume is the era's popular guide to the monsters of the sea.
hartmann-life-of-paracelsus-1887:
Franz Hartmann brought a famed healer back to life in The Life of Paracelsus, his life tale of 1887. Paracelsus was a bold Swiss healer of the age past Luther. He scorned old books, healed with new drugs, and roamed from town to town in search of truth.

Hartmann reads him as a mage as well as a healer. He draws on the healer's own books and old tales of his cures. Fans of the occult in England had scant on him in their tongue. Hartmann's tale filled that gap and made him a hero. The healer's cures were famed and fought in his own day. Hartmann sides with the famed tales, yet keeps the man's grit in view.
waite-real-history-of-the-rosicrucians-1:
A. E. Waite set out to sift fact from dream in The Real History of the Rosicrucians, his study of 1887. Waite was a young clerk with a sage's zeal. He read the old tracts, lists, and claims in full. Then he told what the proof could bear, and no more than that.

His tale is calm and spare next to Jennings's wild one. He traces the first tracts and the men back of them. Later scribes cite his work as their base. It is the sober root of all study of the band. Waite went on to write a shelf of books on rite and sign. This early work shows the care that made his name lead the field.
seybert-commission-report-1887:
Seers faced a stern test in the Seybert Commission report of 1887. A gift of funds charged a great school in Pennsylvania to weigh the claims of the dark room. Horace Furness, a sage of Shakespeare, led the band. They sat with famed names of the day and watched each rite and claim at close hand.

Their first report finds fraud, self deceit, and scant that stands. The tone is dry and fair, which made its sting worse for fans. It is the first such verdict by a school in the United States. Its fame still lasts.
gurney-tertium-quid-1887:
Edmund Gurney seeks a third path in Tertium Quid, his book of tales of thought from 1887. The name means a third thing. Gurney, a chief of the new study of ghosts, balks at two camps: fraud or ghosts. His tracts on trance, dreams that wound, and thought leaps hunt a mid law that could make sense of the scraps that stand firm.

His prose is keen, fair, and hard to fault. Death cut his work short a year past this book. The field lost its best mind young. These tracts are its base in thought.
loudun-devils-1887:
Des Niau saw the strange events at Loudun and wrote them down, and his tale reached English readers in 1887. Goldsmid turned the French text into English for this book. The case centers on a group of Ursuline nuns in a small French town.

The nuns said demons had seized them, and crowds came to watch the rites used to drive the spirits out. At the heart of it stands Urbain Grandier, a priest put on trial in 1634 and put to death. Few tales show so well how fear, faith, and law can mix.
wimmer-runenschrift-1887:
Ludvig Wimmer, a Danish scholar, wrote this study of the rune script in German in 1887. He was the lead rune expert of the Danish school of his day. The book asks where the runes came from and how they changed over time.

Wimmer set the rune rows in order by age and showed how each sign grew from older forms. He used stones from Denmark and the wider north as his chief proof. His scheme gave rune study a firm shape that held for the next age of work. Danish rune work still builds on the frame he set here.
kirwan-essay-on-phlogiston-1787:
Richard Kirwan, an Irish chemist, gave the phlogiston scheme its last great defense in this book of 1787. By then the new French school had strong proof on its side. Kirwan knew that proof well and set out to answer it all. He was no crank, but a sound chemist with a strong name in his field.

He held that phlogiston was a real stuff, bound up with the gas called inflammable air. He dealt with acids too, and how they form and change in his scheme. The book was so strong that the French school felt bound to answer each point in print.
michelson-morley-relative-motion-ether-1:
Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley ran the famed ether test at Cleveland in 1887. Their tool was far finer than the one Michelson used at Potsdam in 1881. They floated the stone base on mercury so it could turn with no jar or shake.

As the base turned, the light bands should have crept if the Earth moved through the ether. They did not creep at all, in test after test, at all times of year. The blank result is the most famed failed trial in physics, and relativity grew from it.
reeves-rothschilds-financial-rulers-of-n:
John Reeves wrote this life of the Rothschild house in 1887, and it came out in Chicago that year. Its bold sub title calls the family the financial rulers of nations. Reeves was the first man to write a full book on the house in English.

He tells of the five sons in five great towns and the state loans they ran. The Jewish Encyclopedia lists his book in its Rothschild sources, as a sound work of its time. The book is a fair, calm Victorian view of the house at its height of fame.
taylor-hymns-orpheus-1787:
Thomas Taylor, an English Platonist, turned the Hymns of Orpheus into English in 1787. It was the first English form of these old Greek hymns. Taylor was a lone, keen man who gave his life to the Greek sages and their gods.

The hymns praise the gods of Greece, one by one, in rich and high verse. With them stands Taylor's own long piece on the life and thought of Orpheus, the famed singer priest. The book is the root text in English for the rites that bear the name of Orpheus.
hitopadesa-wilkins-1787:
Charles Wilkins gave England the Hitopadesa in 1787, the first English version of the Sanskrit fable set. The Sanskrit title page names the sage Vishnu Sharma as its source. Wilkins had learned Sanskrit in India and printed the book at Bath.

A king hires the sage to teach his dull sons the art of wise rule. The sage uses beast tales, each with a moral in verse. Foxes, lions, and birds show how trust, greed, and haste play out. These shrewd tales taught princes and pleased plain readers alike. Wilkins also made the first Sanskrit grammar in English.
chaucer-canterbury-tales-1387:
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in the late 1300s, in Middle English. This text gives the Tales and other poems in D. Laing Purves's standard edition. Chaucer stands as the founding figure of English literature as we know it.

Pilgrims ride from London to Canterbury and tell tales to pass the road. A knight, a miller, a wife of Bath, and a pardoner take turns. Their tales range from high romance to rude and hearty farce. Chaucer lets each voice sound true to rank, trade, and temper. The work opens a full world of medieval English life.
hugo-les-miserables-hapgood-1887:
Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables in French, and Isabel Florence Hapgood made it English in 1887. Hapgood's full version became the standard public-domain English text of the vast novel. Hugo built the book over decades and published it to worldwide fame in 1862.

Jean Valjean, jailed nineteen years for stealing bread, starts life anew in France. Inspector Javert hunts him for years, bound to law more than to mercy or grace. Valjean raises Cosette, joins the Paris rising of 1832, and spares his hunter's life. Hugo pauses for long essays on Paris sewers, Waterloo, convents, and the poor of France. The novel pleads for mercy toward the poor with unmatched scope and heart.
strindberg-the-father-1887:
August Strindberg wrote The Father in 1887, here in Edith and Warner Oland's English translation in print. The naturalist tragedy of the Captain's destruction in the battle of the sexes made Strindberg world-famous overnight. Its three acts compress a marriage's war into one house, one doubt, and one straitjacket at home.

Captain Adolf, a cavalry officer and man of science, fights his wife Laura over their daughter's schooling. Laura plants a doubt about his paternity, and the doubt eats his reason like a slow poison. Servants, a pastor, and a doctor are drawn in as Laura steers him toward the asylum's keepers. The old nurse tricks him into the straitjacket with a mother's soft voice and a nurse's hands. The Olands' version carried this fierce chamber tragedy to English and American stages alike.
engels-working-class-1887:
Friedrich Engels was a young German clerk sent to Manchester to work in his family's cotton business in the 1840s. He walked the slums of the factory districts and wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England from what he saw. This English translation by Florence Kelley Wischnewetzky appeared in 1887.

Engels describes crowded courts, open sewers, child labor, and wages that barely kept families alive. He blames the new factory system itself, not the failings of the poor, for the misery around him. The book became a founding text of industrial sociology and of socialist reporting alike.
russell-studies-scriptures-vol2-1887:
Russell's Time is at Hand, in this 1889 edition of Studies in the Scriptures, Volume 2, works out the movement's Bible chronology. Russell counts the ages from creation forward through dates drawn from scripture and history. The 1914 prophecy stands at the heart of the book.

He argues that the times of the Gentiles, a span counted from ancient Babylon, would end in 1914 with the fall of earthly kingdoms. Charts and parallel dates between Israel's history and the gospel age fill the chapters. Bible Students treated the chronology as proof that they lived in the last days of the present order.
hardy-woodlanders-1887:
Thomas Hardy published The Woodlanders in 1887, setting it in the deep woods of Little Hintock in Wessex. Hardy called it one of his favorite novels. The story grows out of the timber trade, apple orchards, and cider making of a small woodland village.

Grace Melbury, educated beyond her village, returns home torn between two men. Giles Winterborne, the faithful woodsman who loves her, has lost his houses and standing. The charming doctor Fitzpiers wins her hand instead, then proves feckless and unfaithful. Hardy tracks the damage through the seasons. The novel is a tender, sorrowful study of class, love, and loyalty among trees.
mallarme-poesies-french-1887:
Stéphane Mallarmé published his Poésies in 1887, gathering the poems of his career to that date. The text here is the French original. Mallarmé led the Symbolist movement in France, and his poems favor suggestion over plain statement, music over argument.

Among the best-known pieces are 'L'Après-midi d'un faune,' about a faun's drowsy afternoon dream, and the swan sonnet of a bird trapped in ice. His verse is dense, polished, and hard to unlock on a first reading. Patient readers find exact, haunting images of absence, purity, and art itself. The Poésies mark the high point of Symbolist poetry in French.
schiller-don-carlos-1787:
Don Carlos, Schiller's tragedy of 1787, is Englished here in R. D. Boylan's translation. At the court of Philip II of Spain, Prince Carlos loves his stepmother, Queen Elisabeth, once promised to him. His friend the Marquis of Posa dares to plead for freedom in the Netherlands.

Posa's famous interview with the king asks for freedom of thought itself. The Inquisition, jealous courts, and secret police close around them all. Carlos, Posa, and the queen are crushed between love, duty, and power. Schiller wrote the play in stately verse, a step beyond his stormy youth. Verdi later made it an opera, and its plea for free thought still resounds.
heine-prose-writings-1887:
Havelock Ellis edited this selection of Heine's prose in 1887, drawn from across his career. The Travel Pictures, or Reisebilder, mix journeys in Germany and Italy with jokes, dreams, and sudden deep feeling. The Romantic School judges Germany's recent writers with wit that spared no reputation, including Heine's own friends.

Florentine Nights tells eerie tales in a sickroom frame, full of art and ghosts. The Gods in Exile imagines the old pagan gods hiding in a Christian world. Ellis chose the pieces that show Heine the prose ironist at full stretch. The result is a sharp, funny, melancholy tour of his mind. English readers met modern German prose largely through volumes like this one.
leopardi-poems-townsend-1887:
Frederick Townsend translated the poems of Giacomo Leopardi into English in 1887. Leopardi, who died young in 1837, wrote the lyrics known in Italy as the Canti. Townsend's volume holds that lyric work complete; Leopardi's prose dialogues are staged apart from it in the library.

The poems speak to the moon, to Silvia, to his native village, and to his own heart. Love, boredom, lost youth, and nature's indifference are his great themes. His pessimism is famous, yet the verse itself is full of sweetness and light. Italians rank Leopardi as their greatest lyric poet after Dante. Townsend gave English readers the whole arc of that brief, intense career in one volume.
sayce-religion-ancient-babylonians-1887:
A. H. Sayce delivered his Hibbert Lectures in 1887 as Lectures on the Origin and Growth of Religion as Illustrated by the Religion of the Ancient Babylonians. Williams and Norgate published them at London the same year. Sayce, a pioneer Assyriologist at Oxford, read Babylon's hymns, omens, and myths from the new cuneiform finds.

He set Babylonian beliefs about gods, sin, and the soul beside the Hebrew scriptures he also taught. The lectures announced, to a wide public, what Assyriology meant for the history of religion. They were cited everywhere in their day and sparked fierce debate. Sayce writes as a scholar-explorer reporting from a newly opened world. The book founded an English conversation that has not stopped since.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-1-1887:
Henry Charles Lea was a Philadelphia publisher who became America's great historian of the church's dark side. His History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages appeared in 1887. This first volume lays the ground: the rise of heresy, the church's turn to force, and the building of the tribunal. It is the foundation of modern Inquisition studies.

Lea traces the Albigensian Crusade, the papal inquisitors, and the rules of procedure: secret charges, no counsel, torture by law. He works from the records themselves, in a cool and damning style. France and Italy are his chief ground in this volume. The book made his name on both sides of the Atlantic.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-2-1887:
The second volume of Henry Charles Lea's History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, from 1887, follows the tribunal across Europe. Lea wrote from printed records and archives with a lawyer's care for proof. His subject here is the Inquisition at work in Spain's neighbor lands, Italy, and Germany, among other fields.

He treats the Spanish peninsula before its own great tribunal rose, the Italian cities, and the German lands where the inquisitor Conrad of Marburg spread terror. Sorcery and witchcraft enter, as the church begins to hunt them with the heretics. Lea's calm tone makes the burnings and confiscations hit harder. The volume widens his map of fear.
price-review-principal-questions-morals-:
Richard Price, a Welsh minister and philosopher, published A Review of the Principal Questions in Morals in 1758. The third edition of 1787 is the text here, with its appendix and a dissertation on the Deity. Price defends rationalist ethics: moral truth, he holds, is perceived by the reason, as surely as any other truth.

His great opponent is Hutcheson's moral sense, which Price finds too blind and shifting to ground duty. Right and wrong, for Price, are real features of actions, known by the understanding. The Review influenced Kant and steadied the rationalist line in British ethics. Price writes with a minister's conscience and a mathematician's care. His book rewards slow reading.
spr-proceedings-vol4-1886-1887:
Volume four of the Proceedings covers the years 1886 and 1887 in parts ten and eleven. London's Society for Psychical Research kept building its case files here. Thought reading experiments run alongside reports of crisis apparitions. A census of strange experiences was taking shape in these years.

Committees report in dry tables, then argue over what the numbers mean. Mediums who sat for the society include the trance speaker Mrs. Piper's circle and others. Physical wonders, like table movement, face exposure as often as praise. The volume captures psychical research in its earnest Victorian prime. Its records fed arguments for the next fifty years.
gebelin-monde-primitif-vol8-1787:
Tarot history starts in print in 1787, inside the eighth volume of Antoine Court de Gébelin's Monde primitif. His dissertation Du Jeu des Tarots, printed among mixed essays with six plates, first claimed the cards came from ancient Egypt. Court de Gébelin compared the modern world with the primitive one across his huge, unfinished work.

The claim had no proof, yet it launched two centuries of tarot lore at a stroke. Every later writer on the cards' hidden meaning answers Gébelin, knowingly or not. The French text of Tome VIII thus stands as the founding document of tarot history, the spring of the whole occult tradition of the pack.
appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
James Wilson and John Fiske edited Appletons' work, and Volume One appeared in 1887, covering Aaron to Crandall. The whole set holds more than 15,000 lives. It was America's great national book of lives of the nineteenth century.

Entries sketch presidents, generals, inventors, clergy, and artists from the colonial age to the editors' own day. Portraits and facsimile signatures enliven the pages. The editors aimed for a complete record of notable American lives in one alphabet. Family historians and scholars still consult Appletons' for people found in no other reference work of the period. The entries run short, plain, and full of dates that are hard to find elsewhere now.
plos-pone-0003387:
Justin M. Percival and colleagues studied weak muscles in mice for this 2008 paper. Healthy muscle holds an enzyme called nNOSμ at the fiber surface. There it makes nitric oxide, a gas that helps muscle work. The enzyme stays put by attaching to the dystrophin protein complex.

Mice bred without that enzyme developed a muscle disease called myopathy. Their fibers showed damage and their strength was reduced. The loss shows the enzyme is not a minor extra in muscle. Its absence alone is enough to make skeletal muscle fail. Healthy fibers need that gas signal in the right place at the right time.
plos-pone-0003487:
Emilie Bonnet and co-authors tested a vitamin fix for memory loss in rats in this 2008 study. Rats deprived of vitamin A lost ground on spatial memory tasks. New neurons are born in the hippocampus across life and aid memory. Retinoid signals from vitamin A support that birth process.

Giving retinoic acid restored new neuron growth in the deprived rats. Their spatial memory deficit reversed along with it. The work ties vitamin A signaling to adult brain repair. It also links diet to the health of memory circuits. Vitamin A lack is common in poor regions, where diet gaps hit children hardest.
plos-pone-0003587:
Daniel Wegmann, Isabelle Dupanloup, and Laurent Excoffier linked splicing to gene use patterns in this 2008 paper. Alternative splicing creates much of the protein diversity in complex animals. It is likely central to the complexity of higher eukaryotes. Most studies had focused on the molecular machinery that triggers splicing.

The team found the width of a gene's expression profile drives its splicing. Genes used across many conditions splice in more varied ways. How broadly a gene works may shape how many forms it takes. The link connects gene usage to protein variety.
plos-pone-0003687:
Emiliano Merlo and Arturo Romano published this memory study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A memory tied to a place can fade when the place is visited again without the reward or harm that formed it. That fading, called extinction, can also fail, and the old memory can return.

The authors show that extinction requires shutting off NF-kB, a factor that switches genes on. Blocking that factor's activity was part of how the memory lost its force. The result presents forgetting as an active shutdown in the brain, not a passive decay over time.
plos-pone-0003787:
Isabella Santi, Alfredo Pezzicoli, Mattia Bosello, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Group B Streptococcus uses enzymes called pullulanases to break down alpha-glucans, sugars it meets in the human host. Such enzymes may help the bacterium adapt to host niches. Genome reading turned up a new candidate.

The team characterized a newly found pullulanase that sits on the bacterial surface. Antibodies against it could block the breakdown of alpha-glucans. A surface enzyme that both feeds the bacterium and draws immune fire is a candidate piece for future vaccines.
plos-pone-0003887:
Waraphon Phimpraphi, Richard Paul, Bhee Witoonpanich, and co-authors studied malaria risk in Thailand in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article looks at a Karen population living where malaria is common. Past work on host genes mostly sought single genes that protect against malaria. Less work weighed genes against shared living conditions as a whole.

The team estimated how much of the risk for two malaria types runs in families. They covered infections by Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. Splitting risk into family and non-family parts guides future gene hunts. It also shows how much prevention must target homes and surroundings.
plos-pone-0003987:
Jérôme Beaufays, Benoît Adam, Catherine Menten-Dedoyart, and co-authors described a tick saliva protein in 2008. Ticks secrete many proteins while feeding on blood. Lipocalins in saliva help mute the host's inflammatory response. The team had earlier found fourteen new lipocalin genes in Ixodes ricinus.

Their PLOS ONE article characterizes one of them, called Ir-LBP. It binds LTB4, a signal that draws neutrophils to injury sites. By soaking up that signal, the protein interferes with neutrophil function. Such proteins help ticks feed undisturbed for days. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004087:
Philippe Bossi, Frédérick Gay, Imène Fouzai, and co-authors studied smallpox vaccine response in France in 2008. In March 2003, France built a bioterror preparedness program. It formed a national team ready for revaccination against smallpox. Team members had been immunized earlier in life.

Their PLOS ONE article asks which factors predict response to the vaccine. Age, health, and clinical traits were compared with outcomes. Knowing who responds well sharpens outbreak response planning. Such data are rare because routine smallpox vaccination ended decades ago. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004187:
Piotr Religa and colleagues published this transplant study in PLOS ONE in 2009. After a heart transplant, the new organ's arteries can thicken from inside, a problem called transplant arteriosclerosis. The thickening is built from smooth muscle cells that come from both the donor organ and the recipient's own body.

Using 124 heart biopsies, the team assessed how clinical factors relate to the presence of these host-derived cells in the graft. They also weighed the roles of inflammation and a cell-attracting signal called MCP-1. Understanding where the invading cells come from matters for keeping transplanted hearts working longer.
plos-pone-0004287:
Gaby Doxiadis and colleagues published this primate genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In humans, the MHC class I B locus is single and highly variable, linked to a microsatellite called MIB. Rhesus macaques differ: their haplotypes carry unique combinations of multiple B genes, each with its own level of variation.

The team used microsatellite analysis and the localisation of retroviral sequences to reconstruct this region's history. They describe a compound evolutionary history for the macaque Mhc class I B region. Understanding it matters because macaques are central models for immune research and vaccine testing.
plos-pone-0004387:
Empathy is the shared feeling that arises when one being senses another's distress. It can lead to comfort, care, or watchful concern. QiLiang Chen, Jules Panksepp, and Garet Lahvis asked whether genes shape that response in mice. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper compares mouse strains with different genetic backgrounds.

The authors report that empathy in mice is moderated by genetic background. Some strains responded more strongly to distress in others. That pattern points to inherited differences in social feeling. Mouse work cannot settle questions about human empathy. It can show where biology may play a part. The study gives later research a model for testing those genetic effects.
plos-pone-0004487: In 2009, Jansson, Tobias, and Jarefjäll found a gut germ's handshake. Sulfatide recognition by colonization factor CS6 from gut ETEC was characterized. The adhesion's first step was mapped. The finding aids diarrhea vaccine design greatly. The germ causes travelers' diarrhea abroad.
plos-pone-0004587: In 2009, Kovas, Giampietro, and Viding scanned kids guessing hidden quantities. Brain correlates of non-symbolic numerosity estimation in children were mapped. High and low math-ability young brains differed clearly. The neat finding maps number sense wiring. The young kids varied widely.
plos-pone-0004687: In 2009, Ke, Qu, and Rostad read the cancer's epigenetic handwriting anew here today. Gene-silencing marks across the histone H3 were mapped. The marked genes stayed silent for long. The new study informs cancer therapy design today. The key gene control is epigenetic.
plos-pone-0004787: In 2009, Worobey, Fisher, and Cox linked gene variants to kidney decline in women. Genetic polymorphisms and accelerated renal function decline in women were studied. The variants predicted risk well. The study maps cardiovascular genetics research. The filter rate is glomerular.
tyler-contrast-1787:
Royall Tyler wrote The Contrast, and it reached the stage at New York's John Street Theatre on April 16, 1787. Thomas McKee's introduction calls it bright, humorous, and natural, with sharp satire on the follies of the day. The plot sets two suitors side by side for one young woman.

Dimple apes foreign fashion and polish, while the honest American colonel keeps plain manners. A blunt Yankee servant named Jonathan steals scene after scene. He became the first true Yankee figure on the American stage. Light and patriotic, the play announced that a home-grown theater had arrived and could please a paying crowd.
zola-soil-1887:
Vizetelly and Company issued The Soil at London in 1888 as a realistic novel. A frontispiece by H. Gray shows old Fouan warning a child to hold his tongue. The contents split the tale into five parts of five chapters each.

Fouan divides his fields among his children, and the gift turns poisonous. The family tears itself apart over every furrow of the loved land. Greed, lust, and violence follow, in scenes that shocked even Zola's fans. The French title is La Terre, the earth itself. Pitiless and earthy, the book shows rural France as a place where the soil seems to devour its people.
augustine-of-hippo-the-letters-of-st-aug:
More than two hundred seventy letters of Augustine survive in this 1887 volume. The Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series One, carries them in English. Augustine stands as the greatest mind of the early Western Church.

Bishops receive advice, heretics meet debate, and grieving friends find comfort. Hard questions of doctrine mix with the small cares of real people. The saint appears here as a working pastor, not a distant sage. Brilliant and humble by turns, he stays engaged on every page. Few letter collections from the ancient world feel this alive. Readers meet the man whole, in his own words and on his own busy days.
augustine-of-hippo-on-christian-doctrine:
On Christian Doctrine serves as Augustine's handbook for preachers and readers. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the work in English. Its subject is how to read the Bible and how to teach it well.

Augustine sets rules for untangling hard and figurative passages. He then turns to clear and moving speech for the pulpit. Pagan learning, he argues, can serve God when rightly used. All truth, in his bold claim, belongs to believers already. The book in effect invented the idea of a Christian education. Its influence shaped Western schooling for a full thousand years after his death.
augustine-of-hippo-the-enchiridion-on-fa:
A friend asked Augustine for a handbook of the faith to keep at hand. The Enchiridion was his compact and careful answer to that request. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the summary in English.

Faith, hope, and love give the small book its firm frame. Within it, God, Christ, grace, and the last things each receive clear treatment. No wasted words blur the famous clarity of the exposition. New readers of Augustine often start with this short volume. Veterans return to it as the best brief map of his thought. Few handbooks in Christian history have served so many readers so well for so long.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-catechising-of:
A bored deacon asked Augustine how to teach newcomers the faith. On the Catechising of the Uninstructed was his practical reply. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the guide in English.

How do you explain Christianity to someone who knows nothing at all? Tell the story of salvation simply, Augustine answers at length. Adapt the telling to the listener in front of you, he adds. Let joy in the teacher carry the message to the hearer. The result reads as a master class in the art of teaching. Many judges call it the wisest short book on religious education ever written.
augustine-of-hippo-concerning-faith-of-t:
Augustine asks a plain question in Concerning Faith of Things Not Seen. How can people believe in things they have never laid eyes on? The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the short treatise in English.

Everyday life supplies his answers in case after case. We trust a friend's love though we cannot see it directly. We believe past events on the word of those who report them. Countless unseen things are accepted each day without a second thought. Faith in God, he argues, is no stranger than faith in each other. The great theologian appears here as a philosopher of ordinary trust.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-profit-of-beli:
Augustine wrote On the Profit of Believing for a tempted friend. The friend leaned toward the Manichaeans, the sect Augustine once followed. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the treatise in English.

Believe first and understand later, Augustine urges, and do not call it folly. Trust and authority must come before reason in every field of study. Even natural science rests on believing reports we cannot test ourselves. The defense of faith against doubt stays warm and conversational throughout. It ranks as his most accessible work on the topic. Readers meet a patient guide rather than a scolding judge in these pages.
augustine-of-hippo-on-faith-and-the-cree:
Augustine explains the Apostles' Creed line by line in On Faith and the Creed. He wrote the clear exposition for new converts to the faith. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the work in English.

God the Father opens the articles, in the creed's own order. Christ's birth and suffering receive careful treatment in turn. The Holy Spirit, the Church, and the life to come follow after. Crystal clarity marks every paragraph of the short book. For fifteen centuries it has introduced Christians to their belief. Few teaching texts in any age match its calm and orderly survey of what the creed affirms.
augustine-of-hippo-on-continence-npnf1-1:
Continence, for Augustine, means mastery over every appetite of life. Self-control of the body is only one part of his subject. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the treatise in English.

He presents continence as the virtue that makes other virtues possible. A well-governed soul keeps an inner order that spills into all conduct. Desire itself is not denied, but trained and directed toward good. His insight into the heart grew from his own long struggles. The Confessions tell that story, and this work draws its lessons. Profound reading on the discipline of desire remains on offer here for modern readers.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-good-of-marria:
Some critics of Augustine's day despised marriage as a low state. On the Good of Marriage answers them with a firm defense. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the treatise in English.

Marriage is genuinely good, he argues, on three clear grounds. Its goods are children, fidelity between spouses, and the sacred bond itself. Celibate life is honored too, without making marriage a lesser calling. Balance and humanity mark the argument from start to finish. The treatise shaped Christian teaching on marriage for a millennium. Few ancient works on the subject have been quoted or followed as widely since his day.
augustine-of-hippo-of-holy-virginity-npn:
Augustine praises virginity as a high calling in Of Holy Virginity. At the same time he warns virgins sternly against spiritual pride. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the treatise in English.

A humble married person, he says, outranks a virgin who boasts. That sharp reversal keeps the honor from rotting into vanity. Two truths are held together with care across the whole work. Celibacy is honored fully, and marriage is never despised beside it. The balance proved hard for later ages to keep so steady. Readers still profit from his refusal to let a great gift become a ground for pride.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-good-of-widowh:
Augustine wrote On the Good of Widowhood for a widow named Juliana. She had decided not to marry again after her husband's death. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the letter-treatise in English.

He honors her choice while insisting that remarriage is no sin. Practical counsel fills the warm and respectful pages that follow. Prayer, almsgiving, and the raising of children each receive attention. Augustine the pastor appears here at his most tender and personal. Deep respect for a woman's devotion runs through every paragraph. The work also gives a lovely glimpse of family life inside the early Christian world.
augustine-of-hippo-on-lying-npnf1-1887:
Is it ever right to lie, even to save a life, Augustine asks. His answer in On Lying is absolute: no, never, in any case. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the treatise in English.

Relentless logic defends that hard position against every objection. Lies to shield the innocent get the same firm refusal as the rest. Joke lies and hard passages in scripture itself are faced squarely. Many readers find the argument uncomfortable, and that is the point. Augustine will not bend the rule for even the noblest motive. The book remains the classic statement of moral absolutism on truth-telling in the Western tradition.
augustine-of-hippo-against-lying-npnf1-1:
Years after On Lying, Augustine returned to deceit in Against Lying. A new case had arisen among Christians hunting for heretics. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the later treatise in English.

Some believers faked conversion to a heresy to spy on its members. Augustine condemns the tactic without any hesitation at all. The end, he insists, never makes deceitful means acceptable. Even hunting heresy cannot license a lie told in God's name. The protest against noble lies carries real moral force. It comes from a man who knew temptation from the inside and refused to dress it as virtue.
augustine-of-hippo-of-the-work-of-monks-:
Some monks of Augustine's day claimed prayer excused them from manual labor. Of the Work of Monks answers that claim with plain disagreement. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the treatise in English.

Monks should work with their hands, Augustine argues at length. The apostle Paul made tents while preaching, and he sets the pattern. Ordinary work carries a dignity that spiritual pride must not scorn. The practical treatise shaped monastic rules for centuries to come. Its influence runs into the Benedictine pairing of prayer and work. Readers meet Augustine as a defender of common labor against an early form of religious elitism.
augustine-of-hippo-on-patience-npnf1-188:
True patience, Augustine argues, is more than grimly bearing pain. The reason for enduring matters as much as the endurance itself. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the sermon-treatise in English.

Love of God must drive Christian patience, not mere stubborn pride. Endurance for show or spite earns no praise in his account. The line between real virtue and tough pretense is drawn with care. His insight into motives shows deep knowledge of the human heart. Short, searching, and quietly demanding, the work rewards slow reading. It asks readers to test not just what they bear, but why they choose to bear it.
augustine-of-hippo-on-care-to-be-had-for:
A fellow bishop asked Augustine whether care for the dead does any good. On Care to Be Had for the Dead answers him with care. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the tender treatise in English.

Do prayers and burials truly help those who have died, he asks. The dead lie beyond our direct help, Augustine replies in sorrow. Prayer, alms, and the Eucharist offered for them still avail, he holds. His answer founded later teaching on praying for the departed. Grief itself receives gentle and thoughtful treatment along the way. Few ancient works console mourners with such calm, reasoned, and humane warmth as this one does.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-trinity-npnf1-:
Fifteen books make up On the Trinity, Augustine's theological masterpiece. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the vast work in English. Its question is the core mystery of the Christian faith itself.

How can God be three persons and yet one single being? Scripture, philosophy, and the human mind all serve the long inquiry. Memory, understanding, and will in us image the Trinity, he argues. The search runs deep and makes real demands on its readers. Many call it the most profound work of Western theology ever written. Sixteen centuries of readers have wrestled with its pages and come back for more.
augustine-of-hippo-the-anti-manichaean-w:
Augustine spent nine years as a Manichaean before his conversion to Christianity. Afterward he spent years writing against his former sect in answer. An 1887 Fathers volume collects those anti-Manichaean writings in English.

The sect taught two warring gods, one of good and one of evil. Free will, the nature of good, and Genesis all come under review. Augustine answers as a man who once believed the system himself. No critic knew its weak points better than its former insider. His case rests on one God, good by nature, who made all things well. The volume shows a convert turning hard-won knowledge into a lifetime of argument.
augustine-of-hippo-the-anti-donatist-wri:
The Donatists held that sacraments from sinful priests were worthless. Augustine spent decades answering that claim in writing and debate. An 1887 Fathers volume collects his anti-Donatist works in English.

Church unity stands at the center of his long defense. Grace, he argues, works by Christ's power, not the minister's holiness. A bad priest cannot spoil a sacrament he does not own. The fight with the Donatists split North African Christianity for generations. Its outcome defined what the word church means in the West. Readers meet Augustine as a tireless controversialist guarding the oneness of his flock.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-merits-and-for:
Augustine of Hippo wrote On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins early in his long fight with the Pelagian movement. The treatise, given here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation, also covers the baptism of infants. Its central question is simple to state: why baptize babies who have done nothing wrong?

Augustine answers that every child inherits Adam's sin and so needs grace from the very start of life. Human effort, he argues, cannot earn forgiveness; God must give it freely. That claim became the classic Western teaching on original sin. Few early Christian books have shaped later belief more, or stirred more argument.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-spirit-and-the:
On the Spirit and the Letter takes its title from a line by the apostle Paul: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. Augustine wrote the treatise during his dispute with the Pelagians, and it appears here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. It ranks among his shorter and most loved works.

Augustine argues that God's law, by itself, can only show people their guilt and condemn them. Only the Holy Spirit can change the heart so that a person loves what is right. Rules without inner grace fall short, he says, while grace makes real obedience possible. The book became a charter text for later teaching on grace.
augustine-of-hippo-on-nature-and-grace-n:
Pelagius taught that human nature, left to itself, was strong enough to live a righteous life. Augustine answered with On Nature and Grace, a careful reply that goes through his rival's book point by point. The treatise is presented here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine insists that nature is wounded by sin and cannot heal itself. People need grace the way a sick person needs a doctor, not just good advice. Page after page, he presses the claim that no one can save himself by willpower alone. The work states his side of the early Church's greatest debate with unusual clarity.
augustine-of-hippo-on-man-s-perfection-i:
Can any person in this life reach a state without sin? Augustine takes up that question in On Man's Perfection in Righteousness, another reply to Pelagian claims. The short treatise survives here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, drawn from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library.

His answer is cautious: a sinless life might be possible by God's grace, yet in practice nobody achieves it. That is why, he notes, Christians still pray daily to be forgiven their debts. The tone stays humble and close to scripture throughout. Later debates about human perfection kept returning to the careful balance struck in these pages.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-proceedings-of:
In 415, the teacher Pelagius stood trial for heresy in Palestine and walked away acquitted. Augustine, his chief opponent, responded with On the Proceedings of Pelagius, a close review of the whole case. Readers meet it here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine picks apart the trial record with a lawyer's patience, pointing out evasions, soft answers, and half-truths. He argues that the court cleared Pelagius without facing what the man actually taught. The result reads like ancient church politics laid bare. It shows a sharp controversialist at work on the most famous acquittal of his age.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-grace-of-chris:
Two linked treatises by Augustine travel together in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers volume: On the Grace of Christ and On Original Sin. Both belong to his campaign against Pelagius and the teacher's followers. Together they round out his mature case on how grace works.

In the first treatise, Augustine argues that even Christ's human nature lived by God's gift, not by bare human strength. In the second, he defends the reality of original sin passed down from Adam. His point throughout is that no person stands without help from God. The writing is dense, argued with total conviction, and central to his later fame.
augustine-of-hippo-on-marriage-and-concu:
On Marriage and Concupiscence defends marriage from attacks coming in two directions at once. Some critics despised marriage itself, while the Pelagians denied that human desire had been disordered by sin. Augustine's treatise, in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers version, answers both sides.

He holds that marriage is a genuine good, blessed by God and honored by the Church. Yet the unruly desires felt even inside marriage show, for him, that human nature has fallen. The book is among his most personal pieces of theology. Readers of his Confessions will recognize the same struggles worked out here as doctrine.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-soul-and-its-o:
Where does each human soul come from? Augustine admits in On the Soul and Its Origin that he does not know. The treatise, aimed at claims by a young critic named Vincentius Victor, appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Few of his books sound so openly uncertain.

Two views stand before him: God creates each soul fresh, or souls pass from parents to children. Augustine tests both against scripture and finds hard questions on each side. He refuses to pretend a certainty he lacks. The book shows Augustine the honest inquirer rather than the dogmatist, curious and willing to confess ignorance.
augustine-of-hippo-against-two-letters-o:
After their teaching was condemned, Pelagian writers appealed to Rome with two letters defending their cause. Augustine replied with Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, a reply in four books. The work reaches readers here through the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

He brings scripture, church tradition, and close reasoning together in one sustained attack. Again and again he returns to his core claim: grace, not human will, does the saving. The controversy over Pelagius effectively ended with exchanges like this one. Augustine's view of grace went on to shape the teaching of the Western Church for centuries.
augustine-of-hippo-on-grace-and-free-wil:
Monks troubled by Augustine's teaching on grace asked a fair question: if grace does everything, is free will a fiction? On Grace and Free Will, written for those monks, gives his most balanced answer. The treatise is printed here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Augustine answers no. Grace, he says, works through human willing rather than crushing it, so people still choose and still bear blame. God gives the good will, and the person acts with it. The book is short and unusually clear for so hard a subject. Later debates on freedom and grace have quoted it ever since.
augustine-of-hippo-on-rebuke-and-grace-n:
On Rebuke and Grace faces the hardest objection to Augustine's late teaching head-on. If everything rests on God's grace, why bother rebuking anyone for sin? Augustine wrote the treatise near the end of his life, and it appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

His reply is that rebuke itself can be one of the tools grace uses to turn a person around. Being corrected may be the very means by which God rescues someone. The argument is stern, but it comes from a bishop still wrestling honestly with hard mysteries. These pages show his mind working at full stretch in old age.
augustine-of-hippo-our-lord-s-sermon-on-:
Augustine's commentary on the Sermon on the Mount walks through the most famous teaching Jesus ever gave. The Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, and the command to love enemies all receive close attention. His reading appears here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine treats each saying as one step in the soul's climb toward God. Blessings for the meek and the merciful become stages in a ordered path of growth. The result mixes deep theology with a plain guide for daily conduct. For centuries, Christians learned how to read this sermon largely through Augustine's eyes.
augustine-of-hippo-the-harmony-of-the-go:
Do Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John contradict one another? In The Harmony of the Gospels, Augustine sets out to prove they do not. The work, printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, weaves the four accounts into one ordered story of Jesus's life.

Where the Gospels seem to differ in order or detail, Augustine works to reconcile them with patience and ingenuity. He treats each writer as a truthful witness whose account fits the others. The book founded a long Christian tradition of gospel harmonies. It also shows his deep reverence for the text, verse by verse and scene by scene.
augustine-of-hippo-tractates-on-the-gosp:
One hundred twenty-four sermons on the Gospel of John make up Augustine's Tractates, preached over time to his own congregation at Hippo. The series moves verse by verse through the most mystical of the four Gospels. It is given here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine argues against heresies, unfolds the depths of grace, and always comes back to love. Listeners hear the prologue's high claims about the Word and the quiet talks of the farewell chapters alike. The sermons show Augustine the preacher at full power. Learned, passionate, and pastoral, they remain a landmark of early Christian preaching.
augustine-of-hippo-ten-homilies-on-the-f:
Ten sermons on the First Epistle of John, preached during the Easter season, form Augustine's Ten Homilies. Their text is the letter that says, simply, God is love. The homilies appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library.

Augustine lingers over charity until it becomes the measure of everything else. His best-known saying lives here: love, and do what you will. The sermons are short, warm, and radiant rather than combative. Many readers treat them as the gentlest doorway into the mind of a demanding theologian. They reward slow reading, one sitting at a time.
augustine-of-hippo-soliloquies-npnf1-188:
Soon after his conversion, Augustine wrote the Soliloquies as a dialogue between himself and his own Reason. What do I want to know, Reason asks, and he answers: God and the soul, nothing else. The early work is presented in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Reason presses him hard, and the new convert argues his way toward trust in the soul's lasting life. Philosophy here becomes a kind of prayer, spoken aloud to oneself. The tone is intimate and searching rather than settled. Readers watch one of history's great minds thinking aloud in the first months of a changed life.
augustine-of-hippo-expositions-on-the-bo:
Over many years Augustine preached his way through all one hundred fifty psalms. The Expositions on the Book of Psalms gather that life's work of sermons and notes. They reach modern readers in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Part commentary, part sermon, part spiritual diary, the expositions find Christ hidden in psalm after psalm. Augustine reads the whole Christian life out of the Church's prayer book. Kings, exiles, and singers of the Old Testament all become voices of the believer's own story. For centuries these volumes stood as the Church's favorite guide to the Psalms.
john-chrysostom-on-the-priesthood-npnf1-:
John Chrysostom earned lasting fame as a preacher, but On the Priesthood may be his most searched-for book. Written as a dialogue in six books, it asks what it really means to serve as a priest. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition carries the text here.

Chrysostom had dodged ordination himself, and he writes honestly about the calling's terrors and dignity. A priest, he says, must answer for the souls of others, a burden few can carry well. Praise and warning stand side by side on every page. Pastors have read the book for sixteen centuries, and it still makes them tremble.
john-chrysostom-an-exhortation-to-theodo:
When Theodore, a friend of the young John Chrysostom, left the monastic life for marriage and the world, Chrysostom wrote to win him back. An Exhortation to Theodore After His Fall is that letter, in two parts. It survives in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Chrysostom writes in tears rather than anger. No fall, he argues, is final while a person can still repent and return. He mixes grief for his friend with strong hope for his recovery. The letter shows pastoral care at its most tender. It also hints at the heart behind the famous golden mouth of later years.
john-chrysostom-letter-to-a-young-widow-:
A young woman lost her husband, and John Chrysostom wrote her a letter of comfort. His Letter to a Young Widow, preserved in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, tries to turn raw grief toward hope. It is one of his most personal short pieces.

He grants that grief is natural and does not scold her for tears. Death, he urges, is a kind of sleep, and her loss can become a path to spiritual gain. Alongside deep comfort he gives practical counsel about money and household affairs. The letter shows the great preacher working as a counselor, plain about earth and firm about heaven.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-st-ignatius-:
Two festal sermons by John Chrysostom honor martyr-bishops of Antioch: Ignatius, thrown to the beasts at Rome, and Babylas, who defied an emperor. The Homilies on Saint Ignatius and Saint Babylas come from the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Both were preached to crowds gathered at the martyrs' shrines.

Chrysostom tells their stories in vivid, dramatic strokes meant to stir courage in his listeners. He also reflects shrewdly on how martyr tales shape the soul of a whole city. The sermons belong to ancient preaching at full stretch. They make the honored dead feel present to the people standing before their tombs.
john-chrysostom-homily-concerning-lowlin:
One sermon carries Chrysostom's whole moral medicine in a single dose: the Homily Concerning Lowliness of Mind. Its subject is humility, preached with his trademark directness. The text appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Pride, he argues, sits at the root of nearly every sin. The humble tax collector of Jesus's parable goes home right with God, while the boasting Pharisee does not. Chrysostom aims the lesson at respectable churchgoers who need it most. Short as it is, the homily leaves readers with a clear test for their own hearts. It also shows how much weight one short sermon can carry when the preacher wastes no words at all.
john-chrysostom-instructions-to-catechum:
In the weeks before Easter baptism, John Chrysostom preached a course of sermons to new converts. The Instructions to Catechumens preserve that teaching for those about to enter the Church. They are printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He tells the candidates plainly what they are leaving behind and what life they are entering. Old habits, public shows, and loose speech all come under his warning. A sense of urgency runs through every address, since the hearers stand at the edge of a new life. Few sources show so clearly how the ancient Church formed its members.
john-chrysostom-select-homilies-npnf1-18:
No short volume can hold all of John Chrysostom's preaching, so the Select Homilies offer a chosen sampler. Festal sermons, moral warnings, and doctrinal talks sit side by side in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The choices aim to show his range rather than one theme.

Readers meet the golden mouth in many moods across these pages. He thunders against vice, speaks gently to sinners, and opens scripture with bright clarity. Newcomers to Chrysostom often start here before tackling his long sermon series on whole Bible books. The selection gives a fair first taste of why the ancient world prized his voice.
john-chrysostom-two-homilies-on-eutropiu:
In 399 the fallen court minister Eutropius fled to the altar of Chrysostom's church and clung there for safety. His enemy the archbishop then preached over him, in public, on the emptiness of power. The Two Homilies on Eutropius survive in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

All Constantinople watched as Chrysostom urged mercy for the man who had persecuted others. Yesterday's ruler, he told the crowd, now trembles before the altar he once ignored. The sermons count among the most dramatic ever preached. They join a plea for compassion to a sharp warning about how fast fortune turns.
john-chrysostom-that-no-one-can-harm-the:
Banished from his city and his pulpit, John Chrysostom wrote That No One Can Harm the Man Who Does Not Injure Himself. The treatise, kept in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, argues that real harm can only come from within. Exile gave its author every reason to test that claim.

No emperor, slanderer, or prison can truly injure a person, Chrysostom insists, because outer losses cannot touch the soul. Only our own sin does lasting damage. He writes with the calm of a man refusing to be crushed by disgrace. The book's inner freedom sustained him in banishment, and readers under pressure have leaned on it ever since.
john-chrysostom-letters-of-st-chrysostom:
From lonely exile, John Chrysostom kept writing to Olympias, the deaconess who had stood by him in Constantinople. Their correspondence fills the Letters of Saint Chrysostom to Olympias in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. She had been his closest friend and steadiest supporter in the capital.

The letters mix practical advice, spiritual counsel, and plain news of his sufferings on the road. He thanks her, worries over her health, and urges her not to lose heart. Readers meet the private Chrysostom here: grateful, lonely, unbroken, and tender. Few ancient letter sets show a friendship between a bishop and a deaconess so fully.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-statues-:
Riots in Antioch in 387 smashed the emperor's statues, and the city waited in terror for punishment to fall. Week after week, John Chrysostom preached to the frightened crowds, producing the twenty-one Homilies on the Statues. They appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A political crisis becomes, in his hands, a long lesson on repentance, anger, and God's mercy. He rebukes the rioters, steadies the fearful, and begs the city to change before judgment comes. Preaching rarely gets more urgent than a sermon series delivered under threat of an army. The homilies made his name across the empire.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-gospel-o:
Ninety sermons work through the Gospel of Matthew verse by verse in Chrysostom's Homilies on the Gospel of Saint Matthew. The set counts as the largest surviving commentary on a Gospel from the early Church. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition presents the full series.

Chrysostom first explains the text with unmatched clarity, then turns it on daily life without mercy. Wealth, pride, and hypocrisy all come under fire from the pulpit. Ordinary hearers were expected to follow long arguments and apply them at home. For fifteen centuries, preachers and readers treated these homilies as the standard guide to the first Gospel.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-acts-of-:
Bold, generous, and united: that picture of the first Church drives Chrysostom's Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles. He preached through Acts to show his own congregation what the Church was meant to be. The sermons stand in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Again and again he sets the apostles' fiery common life beside the lukewarm habits of his own day. Sharing goods, facing danger, and praying together all become quiet rebukes. Yet the tone stays hopeful, since the same Spirit still works. The homilies inspire and convict in equal measure, which was exactly his aim.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-epistle-:
Thirty-two sermons unpack Paul's letter to the Romans, the weightiest letter the apostle ever wrote. Chrysostom's Homilies on the Epistle to the Romans appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Romans shaped Western theology, and Chrysostom preached it in the East a thousand years earlier.

He unfolds the letter's great themes in order: sin, grace, faith, and the mystery of Israel. A preacher's clarity carries hard doctrine, while a pastor's heart keeps it close to life. His moral applications are famous for leaving no hearer comfortable for long. Generations have ranked these sermons as the classic Eastern reading of Paul's masterwork.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-first-ep:
A divided church, troubled by scandal, received Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians, and Chrysostom preached on it in forty-four homilies. His series includes the well-loved reading of the hymn to love in chapter thirteen. The text comes through the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Factions, lawsuits, and loose morals in Corinth sounded much like problems in Chrysostom's own city. He answers with equal parts rebuke and encouragement, never letting the congregation off easily. His treatment of the resurrection chapter stands out for its hope and force. Few books show practical Christianity preached at so high a level.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-second-e:
Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians is his most personal letter, and Chrysostom answers it with thirty warm homilies. The series is printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Suffering and comfort run through both the letter and the preaching on it.

Chrysostom draws out the apostle's heart: his hardships, his tears, and his tender appeals to a church that doubted him. Weakness made strong becomes the thread that ties the sermons together. A preacher who knew exile himself handles Paul's pain with special sympathy. These homilies console readers who have known hardship in any century.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-galatians-an:
Two very different letters of Paul share one volume in Chrysostom's Homilies on Galatians and Ephesians. Galatians blazes with a defense of grace against legal rules, while Ephesians lifts a soaring vision of the Church. The sermons appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The Galatians sermons crackle with the preacher's own passion for free grace. Moving into Ephesians, he slows down to admire the picture of Christ's body joined in love. Polemic and poetry pair naturally in this set. Readers get both Chrysostom the fighter and Chrysostom the contemplative in one binding.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-philippians-:
Joy written from a prison cell fills Paul's letter to the Philippians, and Chrysostom preached fifteen homilies on it. The series survives in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Its themes suited a preacher who would suffer for his own preaching in time.

He lingers over the hymn of Christ emptying himself, in Philippians chapter two, and over the call to rejoice always. Contentment, humility, and courage under loss fill the applications. The sermons feel warm rather than combative, aimed at steadying ordinary believers. They remain a friendly way into both Paul's letter and Chrysostom's gentler side.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-colossians-n:
Twelve sermons take up Paul's letter to the Colossians in Chrysostom's Homilies on Colossians. The letter defends Christ's place above every rival power and philosophy of its age. The homilies are given in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Chrysostom unpacks the letter's wide vision with his usual clarity: Christ as head of all creation and of the Church. He warns against empty wisdom that shrinks that claim. The set is short enough to read in a few sittings. It is also deep enough to reward return visits for years, as readers have found.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-1-thessaloni:
Young converts in Thessalonica were grieving their dead when Paul wrote them his earliest letter. Chrysostom's eleven Homilies on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians take up their sorrow directly. The sermons appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Comfort rests on the promise that the dead in Christ will rise. Around that hope, Chrysostom urges clean and watchful living while the church waits for Christ's return. He never lets doctrine float free of the mourners in front of him. The result is tender pastoral care from a preacher who believed theology must console.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-2-thessaloni:
Persecution, a mysterious man of lawlessness, and idle members fill Paul's second letter to Thessalonica. Chrysostom answers with five compact homilies, printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The letter tries to steady a frightened church, and so do the sermons.

He calms fears about the end times without letting urgency fade. Then he turns practical: those who refuse to work should not expect the church to feed their idleness. Prophecy and plain duty sit side by side without strain. Brief as the set is, it packs in a great deal of pastoral sense.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-1-timothy-np:
Church order, the marks of good leaders, and the danger of false teaching fill Paul's First Letter to Timothy. Chrysostom, himself a bishop, preached eighteen homilies on the letter. They stand in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A bishop preaching to future bishops gives these sermons unusual weight. Chrysostom spells out how overseers and deacons should live, handle money, and guard the teaching they received. He also warns young leaders against greed and quarrels. Anyone studying how the early Church governed itself will find this series essential reading. Its counsel on prayer and widows' care shows the same care for detail at ground level.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-2-timothy-np:
Paul wrote Second Timothy from prison, near death, with the famous words: I have fought the good fight. Chrysostom preached ten homilies on that farewell letter. The series appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A dying apostle charges the next generation to guard the faith and endure hardship. Chrysostom, who would himself die in exile, handles those charges with special feeling. He keeps returning to courage, patience, and loyalty to the message. Reading the sermons feels like hearing one tested pastor honor another across three centuries of the same hard calling. Few sermon sets carry quite this much earned feeling in every paragraph.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-titus-npnf1-:
Crete needed elders appointed, false teachers silenced, and households taught how grace trains people to live well. Paul's short letter to Titus covers all of it, and Chrysostom preached six homilies on the text. They appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

From a compact epistle, the preacher draws practical lessons for church life at every level. Sound teaching, self-control, and good works done quietly fill his applications. The sermons move fast and waste few words. They carry the trademark moral energy that made Chrysostom's preaching famous, applied to the ordinary duties of a small island church.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-philemon-npn:
Paul's shortest letter pleads for Onesimus, a runaway slave, asking his master to take him back as a brother. Chrysostom needed only three homilies to preach on Philemon, and they appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Small text, large consequences.

The preacher marvels at Paul's tact: no command barked, just love applied with perfect pressure. Master and slave stand as brothers in Christ, a quiet revolution inside a household letter. Chrysostom draws the lesson out gently rather than shouting it. His three sermons remain a lovely guide to the letter's understated power.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-gospel-o:
Eighty-eight homilies guide hearers through the Fourth Gospel, from its soaring prologue to the resurrection scenes. Chrysostom's Homilies on the Gospel of Saint John appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The series was preached to ordinary congregations, not scholars alone.

Signs, long talks, and the farewell words of Jesus all receive patient attention. Against heretics the preacher stands firm; toward seekers he stays gentle and clear. Daily life is never far away, since each doctrine lands in some duty or comfort. This set long held the place of a gold standard for preaching on John.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-epistle-:
Thirty-four homilies take up the Epistle to the Hebrews, with its claim that Christ surpasses angels, Moses, and the old covenant. Chrysostom's series is printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The golden-mouthed preacher faced a text as lofty as his own gift for speech.

His preaching rises to match the epistle's heights, moving from high priesthood to the heroes of faith. Moral applications cut close to the heart, warning hearers not to drift away. Ancient eloquence here serves a single aim: holding a tired church to its confession. The homilies count among the most powerful of his surviving works.
king-gnostics-and-their-remains-1887:
Strange engraved gems, stamped with secret names, angels, and symbols, led C. W. King into the world of the ancient Gnostics. The Gnostics and Their Remains, published in 1887, catalogs those magical seals and uses them to explain Gnostic religion. It was the founding English survey of its subject.

King treats the gems as documents, reading whole systems of belief off tiny stones. Basilideans, Ophites, and other sects take shape through their amulets and invocations. Part archaeology and part religious history, the book defined its field for decades. Its plates still fascinate, and its Victorian enthusiasm is catching. Later scholars corrected much, but they all started where King began.
dawes-act-1887:
Congress passed the Dawes Act in 1887, in the allotment era's full swing. Tribal lands are broken into single-family plots by its terms. The so-called surplus land is then sold to white settlers.

Reformers promised the act would uplift Native peoples into farming life. Instead it became the greatest land theft in American history. Ninety million acres passed out of Native hands in one generation. Tribes lost land, cohesion, and much of their shared way of life. Assimilation as dispossession stands written plainly in federal law here for all. The act stayed in force for decades before policy finally turned.
tower-commission-report-1987:
President Ronald Reagan appointed the Tower Commission in late 1986 to examine the Iran-Contra affair. Former Senator John Tower led the board, which reported in February 1987 after hearing dozens of witnesses. The scandal mixed secret arms sales to Iran with illegal aid to rebels in Nicaragua.

The report traced how White House staff sold weapons to Iran, hoping to free hostages. Part of the money went to the Contra rebels despite a ban from Congress. It blamed a loose management style that left the president detached from his own aides' actions. Reagan accepted the findings and addressed the nation. The report remains the first and fullest official account of the affair.
lotze-outlines-logic-1887:
Ladd translated Lotze's Outlines of Logic, with his encyclopaedia of philosophy, into English in 1887. Hermann Lotze had taught at Göttingen for decades, and his lecture outlines distilled his system for students. Logic comes first in that system, since every other branch of philosophy depends on how we think.

The Outlines present logic not as a bare game of forms but as the study of thought aiming at truth. Lotze adds a survey of the whole circle of philosophy, placing logic, metaphysics, ethics, and aesthetics in their proper order. Ladd's version made the German master's classroom available to English readers. The volume helped form a bridge from German idealism to the new logic being built in Britain and America, and it was widely used as a textbook.
price-evidence-future-improvement-1787:
Richard Price preached the sermon printed in 1787 as The Evidence for a Future Period of Improvement in the State of Mankind. Price was a Welsh dissenting minister, moral philosopher, and friend of the American and French revolutions. His sermons often carried his politics and his hopes into the pulpit.

The discourse reads prophecy and recent history together, arguing that the world is moving toward a better age of knowledge and liberty. Price points to the spread of learning and the fall of old tyrannies as signs of the design. The sermon is Enlightenment optimism at its most fervent, preached as theology. It shows why Price's admirers saw him as a prophet of progress, and why his enemies feared that his pulpit was really a platform for revolution.
northwest-ordinance-1787:
The Congress of the Confederation passed the Northwest Ordinance in July 1787, the old Congress's noblest achievement. The law governed the lands northwest of the Ohio River, the young republic's first great western territory. It had to answer hard questions: would new lands be colonies, or equals? Would slavery follow the flag west?

The ordinance bars slavery forever from the territory, a clause that shaped the map of free and slave states for decades. It sets aside land in each township for public schools and promises fair dealing, often broken, with Native nations. Above all, it lays down the path by which territories become states on full equality with the original thirteen. The charter under which the American West was born governed the making of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin.
