plos-pone-0006587: Deer forage in clever bursts. Focardi and team found fallow deer tune Lévy walk patterns while feeding. The search adapts — grazers' smart steps, tracked, with heavy-tailed steps. Short hops, rare leaps: hit rate weighed, mobile feeders, tuning found, random walks.
plos-pone-0009387: Freezing sperm makes lab breeding possible, but dead sperm from thawing poison the fertilization of mouse eggs in the dish. This study shows that damaged sperm release factors that block fertilization — and that adding glutathione, a protective compound cells make, rescues the process. The findings give animal researchers a practical trick to raise success rates when frozen sperm must be used.
plos-pone-0009487: Even a one-millimeter worm weighs smells through dopamine. This study shows that the worm's DOP-3 dopamine receptor dials down its avoidance of the pungent odor 1-octanol. The paper reveals how a single receptor tunes a simple animal's disgust — a stripped-down model of how dopamine shapes sensory behavior in bigger brains too.
plos-pone-0009587: The Sp family of gene switches includes Sp1, Sp3, Sp4 — and the odd one out, Sp2, which doesn't even bind DNA the usual way. This study shows mice can't develop without it, and their cells can't multiply. The paper reveals an essential role for a protein that breaks its family's rules.
plos-pone-0010387: The uterus rebuilds its lining every month — and a rare side population of cells may hold the stem cells that do it. This study characterizes their stem-like traits. The paper points to the source of endometrial renewal, with implications for endometriosis and fertility.
plos-pone-0010487: Iron is scarce across vast oceans, yet marine bacteria thrive. This study maps how Pelagibacter ubique rewires its genes when iron runs low. The paper reveals survival strategies of the ocean's most abundant microbe. The strategies reveal how life endures in an iron-starved sea.
plos-pone-0010587: In many countries, women are more likely to be obese than men — and the gap tracks childbearing. This study finds that higher total fertility rates go with bigger sex differences in obesity. The proposed link is reproductive biology. The paper offers an evolutionary lens on a modern epidemic.
plos-pone-0010687: Starting HIV treatment in Africa carries early risks. This Zambian cohort study finds blood phosphate levels predict early death on antiretrovirals. The paper offers a cheap warning marker. The cheap test could save lives where African clinic resources are thinnest.
plos-pone-0010787: Female mammals switch off one X chromosome in each cell. This study finds busy gene marks still sitting on X chromosomes in hybrid cells, even with XIST switched on. The paper shows silencing can be leaky. The result sharpens the picture of X shutdown.
plos-pone-0010887: No two autistic people are alike — genes may say why. This study sorts autism's clinical variety by defined genetic subtypes. The paper connects genotypes to symptom patterns. The approach moves autism science toward precision. The sorting brings order to heterogeneity.
plos-pone-0010987: The stem-cell gene NANOG has a second career in the testes. This study maps its distinct expression pattern across mammalian testes, pointing to a conserved role in sperm making. The paper links pluripotency machinery to spermatogenesis. The finding enriches reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0011087: The botulism toxin's genes can hitchhike between bacteria. This study finds mobile plasmids carrying botulinum neurotoxin genes in Clostridium botulinum. The paper reveals gene travel. The finding complicates food safety. The mobile genes mean toxin recipes can travel. The travel widens the toxin's reach.
plos-pone-0011187: Cooperation can emerge even on ever-changing networks. This study models how cooperation evolves on stochastic dynamical networks. The paper reveals network structure's role in altruism. The finding informs game theory and social science. The role explains why helpers persist.
plos-pone-0011287: Pigs and people need shields against tapeworm cysts. This study maps the parts of S3Pvac, a tested shot against cysticercosis, to guide broader tapeworm vaccines. The paper offers a vaccine plan. The finding aids tropical medicine. The aided medicine protects herds and people.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1287:
Shipping chief Land joined Bissell, his ship requirements director, in this message to Acting Administrator Conway on 23 July 1945. The note ran inside the War Shipping Administration, from its head and its hull-counting chief to the man holding the acting post.

The agency's business was the fleet: which ships sailed where, and what the war still needed of them. With one war ended, that business was being rewritten weekly. A joint note from the top shows the rewrite being directed. It is wartime logistics in its own words, filed among the summit's grander papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1387:
A third memorandum by Stanisław Mikołajczyk, dated 26 July 1945, continues the Polish deputy prime minister's papers in the volume. He wrote on the day the Potsdam Declaration went out to Japan. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

While the world's eyes turned to the Pacific, Mikołajczyk kept writing about Poland. That contrast is the point of his file: great events crowded together in July 1945, and small nations fought not to be forgotten inside them. His third paper in three days shows a man using the only tools he had. They were words on paper, aimed at governments that held his country's fate. The run rewards slow reading.
frus-1945-50-intel-d87:
Panuch, a deputy assistant secretary for administration, wrote to Russell on 16 April 1946. The paper moved inside the State Department's administration wing in the spring. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Spring 1946 was the season of transfer and shrinkage for the State intelligence office. As the central group took shape and the department shed wartime growth. A deputy's memorandum to his chief belongs to that grinding work of moving people and files. Readers who stay with these housekeeping papers earn a truer picture of institutional change than the famous directives give. Empires do not fall in a day; they are inventoried, reassigned, and filed away.
frus-1945-50-intel-d187: A short note records a talk held on 19 February 1947. It is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume on United States intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Such notes were made right after a talk, while the words were still fresh. They name the men in the room and the points each one made. That year the postwar spy service was still young, and its shape was still being set.
frus-1945-50-intel-d287:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Assistant Executive Secretary of the National Security Council(Lay) on 9 June 1948. The State Department prints it as document 287 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

A letter fixed a position in a way a phone call never could: dated, signed, and filed for both sides to cite later. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d387:
The Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) addressed a letter to Attorney General Clark on 7 July 1949. It stands as document 387 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1861-d87:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 September 1861. The dispatch is document 87 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams closed September with a report on the state of the London game. No crisis had broken, and that itself was the news. His steady word from across the sea let Lincoln's cabinet turn its mind to the armies, at least for a while. A quiet month in London was the best news the cabinet could get that fall. News by silence is still news, and Adams knew how to report it plainly.
frus-1861-d187:
A letter dated 11 November 1861 went from William H. Seward to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By 11 November the Trent affair was about to burst upon the capitals. Seward's note to Schurz still speaks in the even tone of routine. Spain's reaction to the crisis would matter, and this letter kept the Madrid post primed for it. Spain's voice in the Trent talks would count, since its island lay beside the sea road. Its island beside the sea road made Spain's voice count beyond its strength.
frus-1861-d287:
On 7 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Haldeman. It stands as Document 287 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d87:
On 26 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 87 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d187:
Document 187 is the third of four Seward dispatches to London dated 10 November 1862 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All four went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

By mid-November, word had reached Washington that Britain would not join the French truce scheme. The danger of foreign action was fading, though slowly. Seward still wrote often, because warships for the South were fitting out in British yards. This letter belongs to the watchful weeks after the worst of the crisis passed. London's answer, when it came, would turn on battlefield news ten days old or more.
frus-1862-d287:
A second Dayton report followed on 13 June 1862, printed as Document 287 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two reports in two days often split a formal account from enclosures or private impressions. For Paris in 1862, the private side mattered, because the emperor's real views surfaced in hints. This report, read with its mate of the day before. Gives the legation's full picture for the week before the Seven Days battles changed every calculation. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d387:
Filed as Document 387 but dated 1 August 1862, this report from Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The printers placed it after a later Cameron report in the 1862 volume.

Cameron wrote at the start of August, in the weeks when the Alabama raider's escape from Britain was angering Washington. Russia's ports and courts offered no such grievances. The report's date places it beside Document 386 in substance, though the file separates them; together they give the legation's August account. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d487:
Two days later, on 10 March 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The note is Document 487 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The follow-up came just after the ironclad fight at Hampton Roads, an event that made every maritime nation rethink its navy. The Dutch, with a fleet and colonies to protect, studied such news closely, and Pike needed Washington's version of it. Short supplementary orders were Seward's way of keeping his men current between the long formal instructions. Together with the order of 8 March, this note shows the tempo of wartime correspondence at its quickest.
frus-1862-d587:
Thomas Corwin in Mexico City received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1862. It is Document 587 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward wrote five days after the Mexican victory at Puebla, though the news traveled slowly. His instructions to Corwin had a hard balance to strike. They had to show warm sympathy for Juárez's republic. They also had to make no commitment the Union could not honor while fighting the Confederacy. Corwin also had to be kept from promising more than Washington meant. The letter is a study in restrained diplomacy, from a government that believed in the Mexican cause and could spare it almost nothing but words.
frus-1862-d687: On 20 February 1862, a Mr. De Long wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 687 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed just after the Egypt papers. The evidence names the writer and the date. It does not state the post he held or the place he wrote from.
frus-1863p1-d87:
On 19 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 87 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The middle sheet of a three-letter day often held the meat: a talk set down in full, or a claim worked through point by point. Adams wrote in that pattern through the winter. This letter is the second of his 19 February set. With its mates, it let Seward see London whole for one day, through the eyes of the man he trusted most abroad.
frus-1863p1-d187:
Washington's orders to London on 5 May 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d287: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 September 1863. It is document 287 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d387:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 February 1863. It is document 387 of the 1863 papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Seward kept every note, and the State Department printed the exchange for Congress. Reading Lyons's side shows how the crisis looked from the other desk. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d487:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 1 May 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d587:
Document 587 in the volume is a letter of 15 July 1863 from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d687:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 November 1863. His letter is document 687 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume. Here the voice runs the other way, from the British side of the exchange.

Lyons had to guard British trade and ships while the Union navy stopped vessels at sea. He also had to judge how far the North would go. His notes to Seward put British concerns in plain, formal terms. For a reader, the gain is balance. Set beside Seward's replies, this letter shows both sides of a tense tie at work on the same day.
plos-pone-0000087:
Sarah T. A. Roord, Evelien Zonneveld-Huijssoon, and their team tested a combined therapy for autoimmune disease in PLOS ONE in 2006. In such diseases, T cells attack the body's own tissues. Their approach paired a dose aimed at the specific target of the attack with a low dose of drugs that calm cytokine signals.

Each part alone can be weak or harsh. Together, the targeted part steers the calming part where it is needed, so doses can stay low. The authors report control of the autoimmune response in their test system. The design idea, precise aim plus gentle damping, is a template that immune therapy still pursues for diseases like type 1 diabetes.
plos-pone-0000187:
Yesser Hadj Belgacem and Jean-René Martin published this fruit fly genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. A small gland in the fly, the corpus allatum, makes juvenile hormone. The authors show that the gene Hmgcr in that gland controls sex differences in locomotor activity and body size, acting through the insulin pathway.

How males and females grow to different sizes and move differently is a basic question in biology. The paper ties a hormone gland, a metabolic gene, and insulin signaling into one chain. Because insulin pathways are shared across animals, the fly work offers a model for studying sex differences in growth.
plos-pone-0000287:
Scott Smemo and Justin O. Borevitz published this genomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, on redundancy in genotyping arrays. Genotyping arrays read DNA variants at set positions, and some probes on them overlap or duplicate each other's information. The authors assess that redundancy and what it means for studies using the arrays.

Redundant probes waste money but can also serve as built-in checks. Knowing how much of an array is redundant helps designers trim waste and helps analysts judge data quality. The paper is a practical audit of tools that powered thousands of genetics studies.
plos-pone-0000387:
Jessica Strid and colleagues tested an unusual route to calm arthritis, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Instead of injecting a treatment, they applied type II collagen through the skin, a method called epicutaneous immunization. Collagen is a target of the immune attack in the arthritis model they used, where the body turns on its own joints.

The authors report that skin-based treatment with collagen held back both the start and the advance of chronic collagen-induced arthritis. Teaching the immune system to tolerate its own tissue, through the skin, could point toward gentler therapies for autoimmune disease. The study adds to work on needle-free ways to retrain immune responses.
plos-pone-0000487:
Kevin A. Edwards and colleagues built a reference collection of fly wing diversity, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hawaiian Drosophila are a famous radiation of species, hundreds of fruit flies that evolved on the islands. The team created a database of wing diversity across these species.

Wings record evolution clearly: their veins and shapes vary between species in ways that can be measured and compared. A shared database lets researchers test how wing form evolves and how it relates to each species' way of life. Hawaiian flies are a natural experiment in diversification, and reference collections turn scattered specimens into usable evidence.
plos-pone-0000587:
Eva H. Shang and Irina V. Zhdanova studied how a mother's cocaine exposure affects the unborn child's body clock, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The circadian system runs daily rhythms of sleep, hormones, and activity. Their work shows the circadian system is both a target and a modulator of prenatal cocaine effects. The drug disturbs the system. The system, in turn, shapes the drug's impact.

A two-way relationship is easy to miss if researchers look only at immediate toxicity. Circadian disruption could explain some lasting sleep and behavior problems after prenatal exposure. The study argues for rhythm as an outcome to measure in developmental toxicology.
plos-pone-0000687:
Katsuya Miyake, Toru Tanaka and Paul L. McNeil proposed a new mechanism for a familiar food poisoning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lectins are proteins found in certain vegetables. Eaten in improperly cooked vegetables, they can cause acute distress in the gut. Exactly how they poison people was unknown, and that gap is what the authors set out to fill.

Gut lining cells live under constant mechanical and other stresses, and individual cells are often wounded and repaired. The team's mechanism ties lectin toxicity to that wound-and-repair life of the gut surface. A clear mechanism matters beyond the kitchen: it could explain other protein toxins and suggest how the gut normally defends itself.
plos-pone-0000787:
Daniel Meulemans and Marianne Bronner-Fraser looked to a humble sea animal for the origin of the vertebrate head, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The origin of the head is central to vertebrate evolution, but paleontology and comparative anatomy struggle with it, lacking unambiguous intermediate forms. Much of the head is built during embryonic development from two ectodermal cell populations.

Amphioxus, a small fish-like creature without a true head, is their window. Studying its development can reveal what came before cartilage, the tissue that scaffolds the vertebrate skull. Insights from amphioxus suggest the head's parts were assembled stepwise, from simpler chordate beginnings.
plos-pone-0000887:
Tero Harkonen, Karin Harding, Thomas Rasmussen and co-authors studied who died in a seal distemper outbreak, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Phocine distemper virus swept through European harbour seals as a new wildlife epidemic. Studies of disease in wild animals often treat every animal as the same, yet age and sex can change the outcome a great deal.

The team broke mortality down by age and sex across the outbreak. Those patterns shape what an epidemic does to a population over years, not just in one season. Their work is a warning against simple averages in wildlife health. It also gives seal managers a clearer sense of which groups need watching.
plos-pone-0000987:
Eric Griez, Alessandro Colasanti, Rob van Diest and colleagues measured how breathing carbon dioxide stirs negative feelings, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inhaling carbon dioxide can trigger a panic like state in people with panic disorder. What it does to healthy people was less clearly charted.

Sixty-four healthy volunteers inhaled four gas mixtures in a double dose setup. The team report the negative affect grew with dose and shifted with age. A safe lab trigger for unease is valuable: it lets researchers test calming treatments under controlled conditions. Age effects also warn against treating all volunteers as one group.
plos-pone-0001087:
Xiaohong Zhang and Hung Tseng studied what happens to the cornea's surface when basonuclin is missing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The corneal epithelium, the eye's clear front layer, stays healthy through two processes: cells multiply, and cells stick to each other. Wound repair needs both, finely balanced.

Mice with a basonuclin null mutation, no working copy of the gene, let the pair test its role in living tissue. Basonuclin was already tied to ribosome gene control in skin type cells. Its absence impairing homeostasis and wound repair shows a growth regulator's reach. Eye surface healing is a daily clinical concern, from scratches to surgery.
plos-pone-0001187:
Chronic cocaine abuse is blamed for brain changes that make staying abstinent so hard. Deborah Mash and colleagues measured gene expression in the hippocampus of cocaine abusers, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The hippocampus is a brain region central to memory, including the persistent memory of the cocaine rush that can trigger relapse.

The authors report genes that regulate remodeling of the extracellular matrix, the scaffold around brain cells. Changes in that scaffold could physically alter connections between neurons. Their findings link the molecular side of addiction to the stubborn learning that keeps pulling former users back.
plos-pone-0001287:
The visual world is split in two: each half of the visual field is processed by the opposite side of the brain. Cristian Carmeli and colleagues studied interactions between the hemispheres in the visual areas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Connections between the two sides are abundant near the representation of the visual midline.

The authors describe a novel interhemispheric interaction: modulation of neuronal cooperativity in the visual areas. In other words, activity in one hemisphere tunes how neurons in the other fire together. Coordinating the two halves is essential for a seamless visual field, and this is one of its mechanisms.
plos-pone-0001387:
Peng Gao, Zeyu Xin, and Zhi-Liang Zheng published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how plants balance carbon and nitrogen foods. Plant cells must keep these two in step to grow well. How plants sense that balance was poorly known. The team worked with Arabidopsis, a small plant used in labs world wide.

The authors pinpoint a gene that makes a protein which tags other molecules. They show this gene is key for the plant's response when food balance shifts. Loss of the gene throws the response off. The finding names a core part of how plants tune growth to the food they can get from soil and air.
plos-pone-0001487:
Wei Li and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that maps the human set of E3 ligases. These enzymes tag proteins for removal or for a change in job, and the tag step gives the system its aim. The team listed about 617 such enzymes and their partner parts in the human genome. Most were barely studied.

Among them they found a new enzyme on the cell power unit, which they named MULAN. It shapes how those units move and signal. A full map of this enzyme family gives labs a shared base. It should speed the hunt for drugs that steer protein tagging in disease.
plos-pone-0001587:
Balakrishnan Ramakrishna and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial on a drink mix for severe diarrhea in adults. Standard sugar salt drinks seldom cut stool loss beyond what vein fluids and germ drugs do. A starch that resists gut enzymes had shown promise as a swap for sugar. The trial pitted the two mixes head to head.

Adults with acute watery diarrhea got one mix or the other at random. The team weighed stool loss, time to recovery, and safety. Diarrhea still kills widely where care is thin, so a better drink has large value. Even a small gain per case adds up at that scale.
plos-pone-0001687:
Tapio Mappes and co-authors ran a field experiment on how selection shapes life-history choices in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Negative frequency-dependence favors rare types: when a strategy is uncommon, it does well, which keeps variety alive in a population. Population density can also shift which strategy pays, driving cycles in type frequencies over time.

The team tested frequency- and density-dependent selection together in the field rather than the lab. The full text gives the setup and the animal groups tracked. It also shows how success changed as types grew common or rare and as density rose or fell. Field proof matters here because lab cages strip out the crowding, predators, and seasons that make these forces real.
plos-pone-0001787:
Brian L. Fisher and M. Alex Smith revised the trap-jaw ants of Madagascar in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Species inventories are essential for documenting global diversity and for conservation planning. But inventories help only if the taxonomic work of describing and identifying specimens keeps pace. The revision covers two ant genera, Anochetus and Odontomachus, famous for their snapping jaws.

Working through Malagasy species, Fisher and Smith sorted which are distinct, described them, and built identification keys. The full text gives the species accounts, images, and distribution records. Madagascar's ants are found almost nowhere else, so a clean revision underpins every later study of the island's forests and their protection.
plos-pone-0001887:
Nickolay Neznanov and co-authors compared how two viruses react when a key cell machine is blocked, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The machine is the proteasome, which chops up worn proteins, and many viruses lean on it to copy themselves. The two test cases were vesicular stomatitis virus and poliovirus.

The team added drugs that stall the proteasome and watched each virus grow. They report a split result: the drugs strongly curbed protein making by the first virus, while the second fared in a unlike way. That split shows virus families lean on host tools to unlike degrees. It also warns that a drug aimed at one virus may fail on the next.
plos-pone-0001987:
Annalise Paaby and Paul Schmidt studied a gene tied to aging in fruit flies, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The gene, methuselah, was found because mutant flies with a faulty copy live longer than normal. It codes for a cell-surface receptor, and it became a lead candidate for how aging is set.

The pair asked what the natural variety in this gene does in wild flies. Does each form change lifespan, or death rates with age, in a real way? Lab mutants can mislead, since their effects may not match those of common forms. Testing real variants shows whether the gene matters outside mutant lines.
plos-pone-0002087:
Aisha Farhana and co-authors unraveled a two-way iron gate in the tuberculosis bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Iron is scarce inside a host, and TB bacteria use siderophores, small iron-grabbing molecules, to steal it. That uptake is a principal survival strategy and a virulence factor, so its mechanics are a prime drug target.

The team report a novel exporter-importer system in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and show its role in trafficking iron. A gate that both sends the grabbers out and brings loaded ones in is a neat piece of logistics. Blocking it could starve the bacterium in the lung.
plos-pone-0002187:
Stéphanie Bedhomme and co-authors watched fruit fly mating behavior change fast once a conflict was removed, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Males and females often gain from different mating patterns, a tension called intralocus sexual conflict. It can keep each sex from reaching its own best outcome.

In an earlier study the team had removed female selection pressure in the fly Drosophila melanogaster, freeing males from that conflict. Here they report that reproductive behavior then evolved rapidly. The experiment shows in real time how a tug-of-war between the sexes can hold evolution back, and what happens when the rope is cut.
plos-pone-0002287:
Fabian Saenz and co-authors showed that a malaria protein is required for the parasite to enter mosquito salivary glands. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malaria spreads when sporozoites, the parasite's infective stage, mature in the mosquito gut and then invade its salivary glands. That invasion is thought to depend on parasite surface molecules.

The team studied MAEBL, a protein related to ones the parasite uses to enter cells. They found its transmembrane form is essential for invading Anopheles salivary glands. A step the parasite cannot skip is an inviting target for interventions that stop malaria before it reaches a person.
plos-pone-0002387:
Cabantous and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Stéphanie Cabantous, Yvonne Rogers, Thomas C. Terwilliger, among others.
